summary: Defines the Telnet Output Carriage-Return Disposition option, NAOCRD, which negotiates how the receiver handles carriage-return characters in output. The RFC is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers use different ways to handle the carriage return, which is like starting a new line. This lets them agree. It is now historic.

subtitle: Negotiating how to handle carriage-return characters in Telnet output

tldr.problem: Different computers interpret and handle carriage-return characters differently; some advance one space per carriage-return, others move to column 1, and some require delay or insertion of null characters.
tldr.mechanism: The NAOCRD (Negotiate About Output Carriage-Return Disposition) Telnet option allows the sender and receiver to negotiate which party handles carriage-return processing and how: immediate, with delay, discarded, or other treatment.
tldr.outcome: Telnet partners can agree on carriage-return handling to achieve compatible output display across different terminal types and systems. RFC 652 is now Historic.

today: RFC 652 is Historic. Modern terminals and systems use standardized line-ending conventions (CR+LF, LF alone, or CR alone depending on the operating system) and Telnet implementations abstract these differences automatically. The option demonstrates early protocol design for capability negotiation but is no longer needed in practice.

sections.title: The Carriage-Return Problem
sections.content:
RFC 652 defines the NAOCRD (Negotiate About Output Carriage-Return Disposition) Telnet option, command code 10. The problem it addresses stems from the differences in how computers and terminals handle the carriage-return character (ASCII 13). Some systems move the cursor one space per carriage-return; others move to the beginning of the line; still others require a delay or insertion of null bytes before the next character to allow mechanical terminals time to return the carriage. When Telnet connects two systems with incompatible carriage-return behaviors, output can appear garbled or misaligned.

NAOCRD allows the data sender and receiver to negotiate during the Telnet session which party should handle carriage-return processing and what the disposition should be, ensuring both systems produce compatible display output.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers talk over Telnet, they need to agree on what a carriage-return does. One might add a delay, another might move the cursor differently. Negotiating avoids confusion.

sections.title: Negotiation and Disposition Codes
sections.content:
The option uses IAC (Interpret As Command) codes to negotiate: DO NAOCRD (sender requests or agrees to negotiate), DON'T NAOCRD (sender refuses), WILL NAOCRD (receiver requests or agrees), and WON'T NAOCRD (receiver refuses). Once both sides agree to negotiate, they exchange subnegotiation commands with an 8-bit disposition code indicating the desired carriage-return handling:

  • 0: Command sender alone handles carriage-returns (no delay)
  • 1 to 250: Other party handles carriage-returns with a delay of 1 to 250 character-times or null insertions
  • 252: Other party handles carriage-returns but discards them
  • 254: Other party handles carriage-returns; sender will wait for a character on the reverse connection before sending more
  • 255: Other party handles carriage-returns; sender suggests nothing about method

Two rules govern the negotiation: if neither party wants to handle carriage-returns, the receiver must do it; if both want to, the sender prevails. These rules ensure a consistent outcome regardless of preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: They exchange codes saying who should handle the carriage-return and what kind of delay or skip should happen.

sections.title: Historic Status and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 652 is now classified as Historic, reflecting that modern systems have largely standardized on line-ending conventions and that Telnet itself is less widely used than in earlier eras. However, the RFC provides important insight into the diversity of early computing systems and the need for negotiation protocols to achieve interoperability. The NAOCRD approach—defining option codes and subnegotiation procedures—became the model for many other Telnet options that addressed similar terminal capability differences.

The RFC demonstrates the problem-solving approach of the early ARPANET community: when systems differ, define a negotiation method that lets them discover and adapt to each other's capabilities without requiring manual configuration or universal standards.
sections.plainLanguage: This option is no longer used because computers now handle these details automatically. But it shows how engineers solved the problem when machines worked very differently.
